# Collecting Training Data {#sec-training}

Imagine training a denoising model from paired low- and high-SNR fluorescence images. The training runs without error and your loss curves are nicely decreasing. However, fine structures in the restored images look blurred. You later discover that the sample moved slightly between the two acquisitions, such that the input and the target were not aligned. The images looked sensible on their own, but were slightly inconsistent together. Or consider a segmentation model whose normalization parameters were estimated from the training images. New images acquired with a different detector gain are ten times brighter. They look normal in your microscope viewer, but their values lie far outside the training range, and the model produces poor segmentations. In both cases, the model may still train normally and its loss may keep decreasing. Crucially, there are no indications that would hinted at a misaligned target or that later intensities fall outside the training range. Such **silent data bugs** are a common source of poor model performance and can remain hidden unless you inspect the data and predictions or evaluate the model on carefully checked samples. As model performance depends strongly on accurate and representative training examples [@moen2019; @Hagen2021], detecting and avoiding such silent data bugs is a crucial competence of every deep learning practitioner.

Microscopes are physical measurement devices and the images they produce depend on both the imaging system and the experiment. The optical system, detector, acquisition settings, sample preparation, fluorophores or stains, and biological specimen all affect what is recorded and understanding this helps you recognize meaningful biological variation, artifacts, and conditions that the training data must represent. The goal is almost to **become one with the data**: inspect it often enough that unusual images, artifacts, and mismatched pairs become aparent. This chapter first defines what a training dataset must contain for the intended task and the experimental settings in which the model will be used. It then examines how microscope acquisition and target generation shape the examples, including the pairing and domain mismatches. We next cover dataset coverage and quality control, followed by splitting strategies that avoid leakage and support meaningful validation.

## Planning what to collect

Before acquiring training data, one should consider the analysis task and the experimental conditions under which the model will later be applied. This includes the input modality and channels, what the model should predict and at which biological level, the source of supervision, and the expected biological and acquisition conditions. For [segmentation](2-primer.qmd#segmentation-turning-pixels-into-objects), this includes deciding which structures belong to the target class and how ambiguous boundaries or unlabeled objects are treated. For supervised [image restoration](glossary.qmd#image-restoration), it includes the image property the reference should improve, such as signal-to-noise ratio or spatial resolution, and the required spatial and temporal correspondence. These acquisition-level properties do not by themselves establish whether restoration is adequate for downstream analysis; that requires task-specific output metrics such as those discussed in @sec-output_quality. These choices produce the task-specific data requirements summarized in @tbl-task-data.

| Intended application | Required data relationship | Main planning question |
|---|---|---|
| Classification | Image, field of view, or specimen paired with a class label | What does each label describe: a cell, field of view, specimen, or experimental condition? |
| Segmentation | Image paired with object, pixel, point, or boundary annotations | Which structures count as targets, and how will ambiguous or incomplete annotations be handled? |
| Supervised restoration | Degraded image paired with a corresponding reference that improves a specified image property | Which property should the reference improve, how will this be assessed for downstream use, and what spatial or temporal correspondence is required? |
| Self-supervised or unpaired restoration | No matched clean reference; supervision comes from the input itself or from a separate image collection | Which assumptions provide supervision, and which independent references will test them? |
| Tracking | Time series paired with object identities and temporal links | Which motions, divisions, gaps, and timescales must the dataset represent? |

: Task-specific training-data requirements {#tbl-task-data}

The two restoration examples in @tbl-task-data illustrate how the source of the training signal changes what must be acquired. Supervised learning requires explicit input-target pairs (@sec-supervised), whereas [self-supervised learning](glossary.qmd#self-supervised-learning) derives supervision from structure within the inputs, one of the label-free approaches discussed in @sec-no-labels. Supervised restoration therefore needs corresponding input and reference measurements, while self-supervised restoration can use individual images (cf. @sec-Image-Restoration). *Unpaired* refers only to the absence of sample-level correspondence between collections, not to [unsupervised learning](glossary.qmd#unsupervised-learning), which uses no explicit target labels. Regardless of how supervision is obtained, the collected images must represent the biological and experimental conditions in which the model will be used.

What counts as representative depends on how broadly the model should generalize. A model used only on new fields of view from the same specimen requires less variation than one applied to new specimens, experiments, microscopes, or laboratories. The collection must therefore cover the relevant biological populations, preparations, acquisition settings, and rare but plausible cases. A model intended for use across microscopes requires data from the relevant instruments; additional images from one instrument do not cover this variation. Coverage of the relevant variation therefore matters more than raw image count.

The raw number of images can overstate how much independent information a dataset contains. Experiments contain specimens, specimens contain fields of view, and fields contain planes, frames, or patches. Because observations from the same specimen are correlated, repeated acquisitions are technical rather than additional biological replicates and should not be counted as independent biological observations. The sampling unit should therefore match the level of the intended biological inference and model generalization. Additional independent units and relevant conditions usually provide more information than additional crops from the same source, a distinction that should also inform dataset-size estimates (cf. @sec-9.3.4.5). Independent sampling is still insufficient if biological conditions are confounded with acquisition batches.

For example, control specimens may be processed in one experimental session and treated specimens in another, perhaps by different people or with slightly different protocols. Any resulting differences in sample handling, staining, illumination, or detector calibration are then confounded with treatment and can become model shortcuts. Such systematic technical differences between groups of samples are called **batch effects**. Biological conditions should therefore be distributed across preparation days, slides, acquisition sessions, and instruments, with acquisition order randomized where possible [@bertramDataSetCreation2026]. Stable batch identifiers are needed for later inspection and splitting. (Note that acquisition batches differ from training [batches](glossary.qmd#batch), which are groups of examples processed together during optimization.)

Together, the expected conditions of use, sampling unit, and batch structure determine what must be collected. The microscope and target-generation procedure then determine whether these measurements form valid training examples.

## Microscope-based acquisition and target generation

- microscope and acquisition process as sources of signal, sampling, noise, and artifacts
- imaging domain defined by specimen, microscope, acquisition geometry, and preprocessing
- acquisition settings and metadata needed to interpret and reproduce the measurements
- direct paired acquisitions, informative channels, manual annotations, proxy labels, and synthetic targets
- correspondence and target-quality checks appropriate for the intended task

As mentioned in the introduction, a decreasing training loss does not guarantee that the input and target images form valid training pairs. This can be illustrated with a simple denoising task @fig-training-data-mismatches where we compare denoising models trained with aligned low- and high-SNR membrane images, spatially shifted targets, or nucleus images from a different imaging domain. The aligned pairs produce a membrane reconstruction that follows the clean target. Random shifts make the correspondence inconsistent and blur the prediction. Training on nuclei and then applying the model to membranes produces a prediction dominated by structures learned from the training domain.

![**Training-data mismatches in a denoising task.** Rows compare aligned membrane pairs (top), spatially shifted membrane targets (middle), and train/test domain-shift (bottom). Columns show representative training pairs, loss curves, and predictions for the same membrane test image.](5-figures/figure2.png){#fig-training-data-mismatches}

## Dataset coverage and quality control

- deliberate coverage of biological and technical variation, rare cases, and class imbalance
- distinction between difficult but valid experimental conditions and acquisition failures
- visual and quantitative inspection of raw data, targets, processed samples, and data-loader batches
- pairing and integrity checks for identifiers, dimensions, data types, intensity ranges, and labels
- batch effects, confounding, shortcut learning, and shifts between training data and data encountered in the intended application
- raw data, metadata, provenance, dataset versions, and verified file conversion

## Dataset splitting and validation

- distinct roles for training, validation, and test data
- grouping by the biological or experimental unit at which the model should generalize
- prevention of leakage between neighboring patches, planes, frames, or repeated measurements
- representative test data for the intended application
- held-out experiments, microscopes, or laboratories for explicit domain-shift tests
- frozen split assignments and a practical pre-training dataset audit
